extracted.intended_audience: students of painting (Royal Academy students; aspiring academic painters)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for students training in academic painting: practice, study of masters, observation of nature, and development of an ideal "great style." Emphasises methods, habits, and aesthetic standards for producing high-quality history/figure painting and related genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good colouring (recourse to nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have clearly and distinctly learned in what good colouring consists, you cannot do better than have recourse to nature herself, who is always at hand, and in comparison of whose true splendour the best coloured pictures are but faint and feeble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nature as the primary guide for colouring; compare the work to nature's true splendour to judge colour quality. Even the best coloured pictures will appear faint relative to nature, so continual reference to natural observation is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective copying—copy conceptions not touches
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanical practice of painting is learned in some measure by copying, but select only those choice parts which have recommended the work to notice. Instead of copying the touches of those great masters, copy only their conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make slight sketches of machinery and general management when a model's excellence is in its general effect; keep such sketches to regulate your style. Do not slavishly imitate brushwork; aim to 'labour to invent on their general principles and way of thinking' and 'possess yourself with their spirit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare by making a companion picture (competitive comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enter into a kind of competition by painting a similar subject and making a companion to any picture that you consider as a model; after finishing, place it near the model and compare them carefully together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This side-by-side comparison will make you 'see, but feel your own deficiencies' more sensibly than by precepts, fix ideas by sensible objects, and mingle true principles with your thoughts. The method is severe and mortifying but effective for self-knowledge and advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility before critique
rubrics_metrics.description: To go voluntarily to a tribunal where you know your vanity must be humbled requires not only great resolution, but great humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept mortification and other people's critique as necessary for growth; discovering faults oneself is the first step to improvement and leads to durable confidence from one's own sagacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be your own teacher—active self-instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction forced upon the mind is received lazily and ineffectually; few have been taught to any purpose who have not been their own teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer instructions you give yourself as they are received when the mind is open and eager; self-directed learning tends to be more effectual and durable than passive reception of others' instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select models of established reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to the pictures that you are to choose for your models, I could wish that you would take the world's opinion rather than your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose works of established reputation rather than following your initial fancy; even if you don't admire them at first, imitation will teach you why the world esteems them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style in painting equals power over materials (Carrache as model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style in painting is the same as in writing, a power over materials, whether words or colours, by which conceptions or sentiments are conveyed. Lodovico Carrache (in his best works) approaches nearest to perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emulate characteristics cited: 'unaffected breadth of light and shadow, the simplicity of colouring... and the solemn effect of that twilight' which suit grave and dignified subjects. Study exemplary works to form stylistic ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid idleness and shortcuts; industry is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many teachers who profess to show the nearest way to excellence, and many expedients have been invented by which the toil of study might be saved. But let no man be seduced to idleness by specious promises. Excellence is never granted to man but as the reward of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persevere in habits of industry even without immediate visible advances. Continual application and countless acts (like practice of drawing) are necessary; do not expect quick fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw from memory; keep the port-crayon always at hand
rubrics_metrics.description: After your return from the academy you would endeavour to draw the figure by memory. I will even venture to add, that by perseverance in this custom, you will become able to draw the human figure tolerably correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the port-crayon your constant companion; regular memory-drawing trains facility comparable to learning to write as a child. Acquire this facility early, since it is much harder to learn later in life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer painting studies to drawing when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever an opportunity offers, you paint your studies instead of drawing them. This will give you such a facility in using colours, that in time they will arrange themselves under the pencil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Painting studies teach both drawing and colouring together. If painting comprises both, and a short struggle will attain the same expedition as drawing, then study painting directly rather than partition practice into parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from schools according to their strengths (Venetian/Flemish colouring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who excel most in colouring pursued this method. The Venetian and Flemish schools... have enriched the cabinets of the collectors of drawings with very few examples; their sketches on paper are as rude as their pictures are excellent in regard to harmony of colouring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To learn colouring study their canvas studies and methods—many colourists made designs in colour or chiaroscuro on canvas rather than fine paper drawings. Recognise each school's practices and learn the appropriate techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not depend on genius—assiduity over innate talent
rubrics_metrics.description: You must have no dependence on your own genius. If you have great talents, industry will improve them: if you have but moderate abilities, industry will supply their deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assiduity unabated by difficulty and a disposition eagerly directed to the object will produce effects similar to those attributed to natural powers; work ethic matters more than the myth of genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant mental preparation and vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: Though a man cannot at all times paint or draw, yet the mind can prepare itself by laying in proper materials, at all times, and in all places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be always attentive to your profession: observe nature, examine faces under passion, catch hints from turbulence or deformity, and use even accidental images (e.g., patterns in fire or discoloured walls) as material for imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice yields readiness—do not wait for inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist who has his mind thus filled with ideas, and his hand made expert by practice, works with ease and readiness; whilst he who would have you believe that he is waiting for the inspirations of genius, is in reality at a loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular practice leads to ease; reliance on 'inspiration' produces difficulty and 'monsters'—cultivate steady work habits and technical command so mechanical parts follow without exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great style—seek an ideal beauty beyond individual nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere copier of nature can never produce anything great; the perfection of this art does not consist in mere imitation. The arts receive their perfection from an ideal beauty, superior to what is to be found in individual nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study classical theory (Phidias, Proclus, Cicero) and form an abstract, idealized idea of beauty; design from that central form rather than copying particular natural oddities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire great style via observing, selecting, and comparing
rubrics_metrics.description: These great qualities always operate in proportion to our attention in observing the works of nature, to our skill in selecting, and to our care in digesting, methodising, and comparing our observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although taste cannot be taught by precise rules, practical principles arise from disciplined experience: observe carefully, select what matters, organize and compare observations to build the ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract central form—correct nature by comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: By this long laborious comparison the painter acquires a just idea of beautiful forms; he corrects nature by herself, her imperfect state by her more perfect. He learns to design naturally by drawing his figures unlike to any one object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify common features across examples to form an 'abstract idea' of the species; using this central form, reject accidental blemishes and produce figures that are more perfect than any single original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine varied characters to create the highest perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest perfection of the human figure is not to be found in any one of the classes (Hercules, gladiator, Apollo); but in that form which is taken from them all, and which partakes equally of the activity of the gladiator, of the delicacy of the Apollo, and of the muscular strength of the Hercules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect beauty combines the characters which are beautiful in a species; know the different characters and be able to separate and combine them to vary compositions without losing the general idea of perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude fashion—seek genuine habits of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter must never mistake capricious fashion for the genuine offspring of nature; he must divest himself of prejudices in favour of his age or country; he must disregard all local and temporary ornaments, and look only on those general habits that are everywhere and always the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contemporary affectations (e.g., turned-out feet, erect postures) that are the result of education or fashion. Aim to address posterity, not merely your contemporaries—'In aeternitatem pingo.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the ancients to attain simplicity of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is from a careful study of [the ancients'] works that you will be enabled to attain to the real simplicity of nature; they will suggest many observations which would probably escape you if your study were confined to nature alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ancient sculpture and classical examples as models of the perfected form—the ancients laboured in the school of nature and provide condensed lessons toward the ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for beauty, simplicity, and intellectual grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty and simplicity have so great a share in the composition of a great style, that he who has acquired them has little else to learn. There is, likewise, a nobleness of conception... an art of animating and dignifying the figures with intellectual grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond formal perfection, cultivate large ideas: enlarge your understanding through reading ancient and modern poetry and various knowledge so figures can express philosophic wisdom or heroic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring grandeur into lesser subjects when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If obliged by inclination or circumstance to descend to the meaner walks of painting, bring into the lower sphere of art a grandeur of composition and character that will raise and ennoble his works far above their natural rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower genres (portraits, still life, landscapes, sea-views) have merit; apply principles of grand style and character to elevate them—excellence in small subjects is praise 'in proportion to its object.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm, determined outline and precision in general forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter is to pronounce distinctly, and with precision, the general forms of things. A firm and determined outline is one of the characteristics of the great style in painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even while overlooking accidental discriminations of nature, assert clear, accurate general forms. Express your knowledge of exact form with correctness and precision in all works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand style applies to all parts of painting
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle... that the perfection of this art does not consist in mere imitation extends itself to every part of the art; it gives what is called the grand style to invention, to composition, to expression, and even to colouring and drapery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and rank of art are proportionate to mental labour; strive to apply the grand style across invention, composition, expression, colouring, and drapery to elevate the painting from ornament to liberal art.
